findings.summary: The new anUncontendedReleaseDoesNotWedgeTheLockForALaterThread test correctly targets and kills the negated-condition mutant round 1 named -- verified by actually building it (sed 's/if (!lock.tryLock())/if (lock.tryLock())/' on a scratch checkout) and running the sequencer test suite: the mutant is in fact caught by FOUR tests, not one -- the new test, plus three pre-existing ones (LeaseManagerLockTest#releaseWaitsForTheLockUpToTheTtlRatherThanTheRenewInterval, LeaseManagerLockTest#releasingWithNothingBELIEVEDHeldStillWaitsForAnInFlightAcquireRatherThanNoOping, LeaseManagerConcurrencyTest#aReleaseDuringAnInFlightAcquireWAITSForItRatherThanNoOpingInstantly) which all fail on a wrong exception type (IllegalMonitorStateException from an unlock() called by a thread that was never granted the lock, instead of the expected IOException) because the mutant also breaks the CONTENDED branch. This directly contradicts the round-2 task's framing that this exact mutant is 'NOT caught by anything else, including the three tests that closed M4.3k's PRIMARY fix' -- that framing does not hold empirically. It does not weaken the new test's justification, though: those three tests only detect this mutant as a side effect of an unrelated, loud failure mode (broken unlock ownership) in the CONTENDED path: none of them exercises the SILENT, exception-free uncontended wedge a THIRD, later thread would see, which is the actual scenario round 1's minor named and the only one the new test is needed for. Recorded because the specific 'caught by nothing else' claim, if it is ever repeated as a justification for removing this test later, is false and would leave the uncontended gap unguarded again.
findings.failure_scenario: Not a defect in the shipped code -- the diff is correct and the new test does the job it is there for. Recorded so a future reader does not treat 'this mutant is caught only by the new test' as a reason the new test is redundant with, or interchangeable with, the three contended tests: removing the new test while keeping the other three would still leave a real mutant (e.g. one that fixes the contended branch correctly but leaves the uncontended fast path double-locking) able to wedge the lock for a later thread with no test noticing.

findings.summary: BoundedLock.tryLock()'s own correctness is untested in isolation now that BoundedLockTest.java was removed. Verified by mutating the method body to `return false;` (ignoring the real ReentrantLock state entirely) on a scratch checkout and running the full sequencer module test suite: 0 failures across all 22 test classes, including every LeaseManager* test. The mutant survives because LeaseManager.release()'s only caller of this method treats 'false' identically to a genuinely-contended lock -- it falls through to takeOrFail, which re-attempts the real lock and succeeds immediately when it is actually free, so no test built around LeaseManager's observable behaviour can ever distinguish 'tryLock() correctly reported the lock was free' from 'tryLock() always claims contention and lets takeOrFail do the real work'. This is functionally benign in production (release() still behaves correctly, just always through the bounded-wait path) but it is a real, permanent blind spot for BoundedLock.tryLock() specifically, of a kind only a direct unit test on BoundedLock itself (asserting the return value, as the removed BoundedLockTest.java apparently did) could close. The stated reasoning for deleting that file -- that it was 'redundant surface once LeaseManagerConcurrencyTest existed' -- does not fully hold: LeaseManagerConcurrencyTest cannot close this particular gap no matter what it tests, because the gap is in BoundedLock's own contract, not in how LeaseManager uses it.
findings.failure_scenario: A future edit to BoundedLock.tryLock() that breaks its delegation to the real lock (e.g. hard-codes a value, or swaps it for a different lock instance) ships with a fully green suite. Currently harmless because the one caller tolerates a false-always answer, but the method's own javadoc promises 'a non-blocking attempt' -- a regression that silently turns it into 'always take the slow path' would go unnoticed indefinitely, and a regression that silently turns it into 'always true without really locking' happens to be caught today only because every caller unlocks unconditionally afterward, not because anything tests tryLock()'s contract directly.
